prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, and dynamic models of industries

statement.case_for: The random-coefficients demand framework (Berry 1994; Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1995), together with Pakes's dynamic-industry work, made it possible to estimate substitution patterns, market power and welfare on real market data. It is used in merger review, antitrust, regulation, trade, health and environmental economics. It is an example of theory built to be tested on data and then adopted in practice. The core papers are thirty years old, so there is a long record of replication, software implementation and methodological critique. The three-name BLP core is compact and well defined, and the field has no earlier laureate. After the opening round I still rank it first on originality, breadth of use and maturity. B025 (Melitz, Helpman) is a very close second on those criteria, and I would not call the choice between them clear-cut.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Seven names are credited, and a three-person cap leaves out Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, whose contributions to empirical IO, to identification of market power and to dynamic-game estimation are real. A prize could look arbitrary if it is read as rewarding a toolkit rather than a single discovery. Identification in structural models also rests on strong functional-form and equilibrium assumptions. In addition, this candidate has less opening breadth than B002 and B025 (7 members ranked it, against 11 for each of the other two), so it may be a narrower consensus choice.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B012 first. He sees BLP and Ericson-Pakes as a methodological contribution with reach well beyond one subfield, but he notes that a three-name limit omits real contributors such as Bresnahan and Reiss.
responses.response: I agree on both points, and the omission is the main cost of my preferred configuration. I read the BLP demand-estimation core, with Pakes's dynamic-industry work, as the identifiable discovery. Bresnahan's and Reiss's earlier contributions are foundational for empirical IO as a field, but they are less tied to this particular estimation breakthrough. Where I differ is that I would not describe the cap as a defect of the candidate itself. It is a constraint that every multi-contributor candidate on the shortlist faces, and B043 faces it much more severely.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 first with Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He argues that collateral constraints are conceptually foundational, with policy influence after 2008. He ranks B012 fourth and flags that Bresnahan's earlier work and the weight given to methodological tools relative to substantive discovery are open questions.
responses.response: I accept that Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean, original mechanism, and I put it in my own top five and added Gertler. My reservation is not about conceptual quality. First, the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises has already covered adjacent ground, and the accelerator lineage runs through Bernanke. Second, the direct empirical identification of the collateral amplification channel is less settled than the theory's influence suggests. On the tools-versus-discovery point, I would say BLP is both. It is a method, and it has changed what we know about market power, welfare and merger effects in actual industries. That is evidence of discovery through measurement, not only of technique.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B025 first and a Melitz-Helpman pairing as the cleanest attribution. He cites over twenty years of confirmation and reach into IO, macro and development. He also flags the partial overlap with Krugman's 2008 prize and the absence of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum from the credited names.
responses.response: I largely agree with his assessment of Melitz-Helpman, which is why B025 is my first alternative. It is a two-person attribution that is arguably cleaner than my three-person BLP set. Where I give B012 a slight edge is on two points. The credited set for B025 omits contemporaneous contributors (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum), which he also notes. And B025 sits closer to the 2008 prize on trade. Neither point is decisive, and I would support B025 if the Committee preferred it.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B012 fifth. He accepts that the BLP and dynamic-industry toolkit is very broad in use, but he is concerned about attribution spread over a large IO group and about ongoing debates on the robustness of structural assumptions.
responses.response: Both concerns are fair. I would respond that the identification and robustness debates (instruments, computational issues, functional form) have been active for three decades, and the method has remained standard through them. That is a sign of maturity, not fragility. On attribution spread, I think the answer is to anchor the award on the demand-estimation core rather than to claim the whole new empirical IO tradition, and the citation I propose is worded that way.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee should add or substitute Bresnahan (or Reiss) for earlier empirical IO foundations, since I rely on my own recollection of the attribution split and have not verified sources.
Whether the Committee would treat this as an industrial-organisation discovery or as an econometric-methods contribution, and how that framing would affect its standing against B002 and B025.
How much weight the overlap with the 2022 financial-crises prize should carry against B002, and the overlap with the 2008 trade prize against B025.
Whether the credited set for B025 should be widened to include Bernard, Eaton, Jensen or Kortum, who are not on the ballot.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of the shortlisted candidates appears among the co-authors listed in my profile. My committee overlap with colleagues is not a candidate-specific connection, and my corporate-finance field is not adjacent to any shortlisted candidate.
